name: ollama

facts.description: Get up and running with Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, Qwen, Gemma and other models.

title: Ollama: A Local AI Inference Engine and Model Serving Runtime
answer: Ollama is an open source runtime written in Go, made by Ollama and released under the MIT licence, that downloads, runs and serves large language and multimodal models on your own machine or in its cloud. It sits at the inference and serving layer of the AI stack, behind coding assistants, agents and chat apps. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its strength is fast, simple local serving rather than training or fine-tuning.

sections.body: Ollama is an inference engine and model serving runtime maintained by the company of the same name, written in Go and released under the MIT licence, with its source at github.com/ollama/ollama and its official site at ollama.com. It occupies the serving layer of the AI stack: it takes model weights, loads them onto local hardware or its cloud, and exposes them to applications through a command line and an API. The site's blog describes it as serving 8.9 million developers and having raised 88 million dollars from Benchmark, Theory Ventures, 8VC, Y Combinator and angel investors. It is not a training framework, and the official material describes no training or fine-tuning workflow of its own.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Its concrete job is running models for inference. The library page catalogues the models it can pull and run, including Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Granite, SmolLM2, OLMo 2, LLaVA and embedding models such as BGE-M3 and Snowflake's text embedding suite. The blog shows it being used for coding assistants, agentic workflows, web search, decision models that answer yes-or-no questions and scores, and safety classification through gpt-oss-safeguard. It is strongest where a developer wants a capable open model running locally with little setup, and the site notes that small models suit entry-level hardware. Cloud models are offered in preview for larger models on datacenter-grade hardware.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The site presents Ollama as approachable rather than academic. The ollama launch command is described as setting up and running coding tools such as Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex with local or cloud models, with no environment variables or config files needed, and the Continue guest post walks through a code assistant setup step by step. No mathematics or machine learning background is described as a prerequisite. What a beginner does need is a machine with enough memory and, for larger models, a suitable GPU, since the Continue post notes that a 22B model requires a lot of VRAM. The official material does not state formal prerequisites, so any stronger claim about required systems knowledge would go beyond what the site says.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around it is broad and documented on the site. It integrates with Claude Desktop as a third-party gateway provider, with Claude Code through the Anthropic Messages API, with OpenAI's Codex CLI, with OpenJarvis for personal agents, with OpenClaw for messaging-based assistants, and with Continue for in-editor coding help. It works with llama.cpp for GGUF compatibility and with Apple's MLX framework on Apple silicon, and it has partnerships with NVIDIA around DGX Spark and with OpenAI and ROOST on safety models. Documentation lives on the site and in the repository, and the project's popularity, with over 182,000 stars on GitHub, indicates a large community, though the official pages do not quantify forum or chat support.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Ollama is built for both quick experiments and serious serving, and the site shows the trade-offs. On the prototyping side, a single command pulls and runs a model, and the Continue post shows several models running concurrently for autocomplete and chat. On the production side, version 0.30 brought improved performance and GGUF compatibility, a new scheduling system reduces out-of-memory crashes and maximizes GPU utilization on multi-GPU systems, and the MLX engine on Apple silicon is described as up to 90 percent faster with coding agents on the Aider polyglot benchmark. The cost is that performance depends heavily on your hardware, and the site notes that client-side inference can be slower on limited machines.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site supports the claim that Ollama is a current standard rather than a legacy choice. It reports 8.9 million developers, venture backing, and partnerships with NVIDIA, OpenAI and Stanford's Hazy Research lab, and it lists current models such as Gemma 4, GLM-4.6, Qwen3-Coder and MiniMax M2 arriving on the platform. For someone choosing what to learn, that suggests skills in running and serving open models locally transfer to agent and coding-assistant work. The official material does not name specific employers hiring for Ollama experience or describe certification, so career claims beyond general relevance are not settled by the site.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Ollama is written in Go and is typically driven from a shell or from application code in any language that can call an HTTP API, which the site demonstrates through integrations with Python-based tools such as LangChain in the web apps guest post and with TypeScript tooling in the browser example. It sits in a polyglot pattern where the runtime handles model loading and scheduling while surrounding frameworks handle retrieval, agents and user interfaces. It is compatible with the Anthropic Messages API and with OpenAI's Codex CLI, so it can stand in for hosted providers behind tools written against those interfaces, and it complements rather than replaces libraries such as llama.cpp and MLX, which it uses as backends.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about some limits and silent on others. Local inference is bounded by the user's hardware, and the browser-based example notes slower inference on weaker machines. Some models carry restrictions, such as Codestral's non-production licence, and cloud models are still described as a preview. The official material does not describe training or fine-tuning support, does not give detailed benchmark methodology beyond pointing to partner blog posts, and does not state system requirements in one consolidated place. Questions about long-term support, enterprise compliance beyond the stated zero data retention policy, and comparative performance against other runtimes are not settled by the pages read.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
